claims.statement: Excavations at Danebury revealed roundhouses.
At Danebury, grain was kept in storage buildings and sealed pits.

value.text: At Danebury, grain was kept in storage buildings and sealed pits.

claims.statement: Danebury’s farming community kept sheep and cattle.

value.text: Danebury’s farming community kept sheep and cattle.

claims.statement: Evidence at Danebury includes cereal processing, weaving, leatherworking and metalworking.

value.text: Evidence at Danebury includes cereal processing, weaving, leatherworking and metalworking.

claims.statement: Danebury obtained materials including metals and salt through exchange with other areas.

value.text: Danebury obtained materials including metals and salt through exchange with other areas.

claims.statement: Four rectangular structures at Danebury have been interpreted as shrines.

value.text: Four rectangular structures at Danebury have been interpreted as shrines.

claims.statement: Published accounts differ: Ford and Saunders use 550–100 BCE for Danebury, while Büster dates its construction around 470 BCE.

value.text: Published accounts differ: Ford and Saunders use 550–100 BCE for Danebury, while Büster dates its construction around 470 BCE.

claims.disputeNote: Chronologies differ; no averaged or exact foundation date is inferred.

claims.statement: The Danebury map marker uses the Atlas of Hillforts site reference.

start.original: Published construction chronologies: 550 or around 470 BCE

claims.statement: Broxmouth’s modelled occupation start is 640–570 BCE at 68% probability.
Broxmouth’s modelled abandonment is 155–210 CE at 68% probability.
Broxmouth’s occupation sequence includes both enclosed and unenclosed settlement phases.

value.text: Broxmouth’s occupation sequence includes both enclosed and unenclosed settlement phases.

claims.statement: Heritage Ireland uses 500 BCE–400 CE as its Iron Age overview period.

value.text: Heritage Ireland uses 500 BCE–400 CE as its Iron Age overview period.

claims.statement: Older monuments continued to be repurposed during the Irish Iron Age.

value.text: Older monuments continued to be repurposed during the Irish Iron Age.

claims.statement: The Atlas reports a start estimate of about 410–375 BCE for Castell Henllys.
The Atlas reports an end estimate of about 380–190 BCE for this hillfort phase.
The Atlas describes evidence of metalworking and interprets Castell Henllys as probably supporting a wealthy farming community.

value.text: The Atlas describes evidence of metalworking and interprets Castell Henllys as probably supporting a wealthy farming community.

claims.statement: The map uses the Atlas site reference for Castell Henllys in Pembrokeshire.
The museum guide describes two wooden wheels from a cart used in the fourth century BCE at Doogarrymore, associated with a trackway.
The Geological Survey Ireland report dates the oak-plank trackway to 148–147 BCE and says it was built in a single year.

date.original: 148–147 BC; constructed in a single year

claims.statement: Raftery’s excavation report dates Corlea 1 to 148 BCE using dendrochronological analysis.

value.text: Raftery’s excavation report dates Corlea 1 to 148 BCE using dendrochronological analysis.

claims.statement: The purpose of the Corlea trackway is uncertain; the geological report discusses a possible ritual use.

value.text: The purpose of the Corlea trackway is uncertain; the geological report discusses a possible ritual use.

claims.statement: The Corlea map marker uses the excavation report’s site coordinates.

evidence.note: Finds span the site’s occupation; not all houses were contemporary.
Site-level Iron Age context; phase-specific dating remains to be checked.
Site-level context, not a description of every community in Britain.

evidence.note: Activities are not yet assigned to individual occupation phases.
The inspected account does not identify all trading partners or dates.
An interpretation of structures, not certain identification of religious practice in a particular year.
The two chronologies are retained. This review does not select a definitive construction year.
Construction around 470 BCE; retained alongside the older chronology.
Rounded to five decimal places. A site reference, not a person’s whereabouts or a territorial boundary.
Bayesian model of calibrated radiocarbon dates; not an exact founding year.
Probability applies to the modelled abandonment estimate.
Changes occurred at different times; the full sequence is not simultaneous.
A conventional period definition rather than a precisely dated nationwide transition.
